sizeReason: Adam, Sara and Yassine have 144 hours across 6 weeks. A short, complete plan fits a browser app for teachers’ laptops and students’ phones. Keep statistics, email alerts and a native app for later. Include security for student data and the EU storage rule, architecture for free hosting and school Wi-Fi, and design for simple screens.

parts.summary: Build a simple attendance website for 40 teachers and 1,200 students. Start with a small classroom pilot.
parts.details:
Adam uses JavaScript for browser interactions. Sara uses Python and SQL for attendance rules and storage. Yassine uses HTML/CSS for pages that resemble the school’s site. React is not needed.

The team has 144 hours across 42 days and no spending budget. Plan 100 hours, including 12 hours of learning. Adam has 33 planned hours and 15 hours reserved for problems. Sara has 33 planned hours and 15 reserved. Yassine has 34 planned hours and 14 reserved. Each stays within 48 hours. The 44 reserved hours are not available for extra features.

Confirm approved EU hosting, school login and school Wi-Fi access in week 1. Use invented student records until real-data use is approved.

parts.summary: Deliver sessions, timed check-in, a live teacher list with corrections, and CSV export. Include login, class permissions and roster loading.
parts.details:
Week 1: agree attendance rules and example data; learn the framework; check hosting, school login and Wi-Fi. Week 2: complete basic login, roster membership and teacher-assignment checks alongside sessions and check-in. Week 3: demonstrate the protected end-to-end attendance flow. Week 4: finish corrections and export; test denied access more broadly. Week 5: run an approved small pilot and rehearse the demo. Week 6: repeat relevant checks, fix problems and demonstrate on day 42. No new features.

Completion checks:
1. An assigned teacher opens a session for the correct class. Reloading shows the same session, roster and server-set deadline exactly ten minutes after opening.
2. A signed-in enrolled student can check in before the deadline. At or after the deadline, the server rejects check-in. An unenrolled student is rejected. Repeated submissions create only one record.
3. Under the approved pilot load on school Wi-Fi, a saved check-in appears in the teacher list within five seconds. A lost connection shows a stale-list warning.
4. An assigned teacher saves a correction with a reason. Reloading preserves it and its editor and time.
5. CSV download contains the selected class session, its complete roster and current attendance, including corrections. Another class’s records are absent. Spreadsheet formula-like values are handled safely.
6. Students cannot read teacher lists or exports. Teachers cannot manage unassigned classes. Test these by sending requests directly, not just by hiding buttons.

Propose a pilot of one class, at most 30 students and one teacher view. This is a test target, not a proven capacity. Use invented data if access, hosting or testing remains unresolved. Statistics, absence emails and a native app wait. If behind schedule, cut QR generation, polish and pilot breadth before required features or access checks.

parts.summary: One 100-hour work budget covers implementation, learning, security and design.
parts.details:
The task allocations below are the shared budget. Security’s 28 hours and design’s 24 hours are included within these tasks, not added to them. The first nine tasks total 70 hours: Adam 24, Sara 33 and Yassine 13. The remaining page and usability tasks add Adam 9 and Yassine 21.

Record hours each week. Any local-password system needs a separate estimate with named owners before it can replace school login. Do not silently spend the reserved hours on that scope.

options.good: All teachers and students can benefit immediately.

parts.summary: Use Django, a Python web framework, with HTML pages, small JavaScript functions and SQLite, a database kept in one file.
parts.details:
Sara’s Python and SQL fit the server. Adam’s JavaScript fits check-in feedback and list updates. Yassine’s HTML/CSS fits shared page templates. Keep one project and one deployment. Skip React, separate front-end builds, microservices and Kubernetes.

Django is new to the stated team. T2 includes four learning hours per person. These 12 hours sit inside the 100 planned hours. They do not turn the 44-hour reserve into available feature time. T1–T9 cover 70 hours of setup and implementation: Sara 33, Adam 24 and Yassine 13. Page work adds Adam 9 and Yassine 21, giving totals of 33, 33 and 34 respectively.

Prefer a free school-managed EU server, confirmed in week 1. PythonAnywhere’s EU free service is a conditional demo option. Its published limits include one worker, 512 MiB storage and one-month web-app expiry; new free accounts have no scheduled tasks. Confirm outbound access for school login too. [Free account limits](https://help.pythonanywhere.com/pages/FreeAccountsFeatures/) and [EU service details](https://eu.pythonanywhere.com/pricing/).

parts.summary: One server handles login, sessions, check-ins, corrections and exports. The teacher list must show saved changes within five seconds under the tested pilot load.
parts.details:
An assigned teacher opens a session linked to a roster snapshot. The server records opening time and a ten-minute deadline. A signed-in student submits a session code. The server checks membership and time before saving. A database rule permits one attendance record per student per session, making retries safe. Teachers can correct attendance with a reason; save the editor and time.

Polling means the browser repeatedly asks the server for updates. Poll every four seconds while the teacher view is active, leaving about one second for response and rendering within the five-second acceptance target. Avoid overlapping requests and stop when the view closes. Refresh immediately when returning to the page. Show the last successful refresh and connection failures. Test the actual five-second result; the timer alone is not proof.

Keep deadline, permission and CSV rules in small pure functions: data in, result out. Database access, network calls and reading the clock belong around those functions. Pass server time into the rules. Keep files below about 400 lines and reuse shared logic.
parts.diagram:
Student phone ── login + check-in ──┐
Teacher laptop ── open/fix/export ──┼── HTTPS ── Django ── SQLite
Teacher laptop ── poll every 4s ────┘                      │
                                                 EU backup storage

parts.summary: Keep accounts, rosters, attendance, logs and backups in approved EU locations. Measure storage before allowing real use.
parts.details:
Tables hold users and roles, classes, teacher assignments, enrolments, sessions, attendance and correction history. Snapshot the roster at session opening so later enrolment changes do not rewrite history. Collect school identifiers and names; add email only if login needs it. Do not collect location or device fingerprints. Keep names and session codes out of logs.

School login is the conditional first choice. Django handles app sessions and request protection; it does not by itself provide school identity integration or failed-login limits. If school login is unavailable, use invented demo accounts. Real local accounts require a revised budget for school provisioning, slow password hashing, verified recovery and support, with named owners.

Sizing assumptions, to confirm with the school: 40 sessions per teaching day, 30 students per session, 100 retained teaching days. That gives 4,000 sessions and 120,000 attendance rows. Allow another 120,000 roster-snapshot rows and corrections on 10% of attendance rows, or 12,000 correction rows. At a provisional 512 bytes per row including indexes, these 252,000 rows need about 123 MiB. Allow 27 MiB for users, sessions and spare database space: about 150 MiB total. Measure a seeded database to replace this estimate.

Against a 512 MiB host allowance, budget 150 MiB for the live database, 150 MiB for one temporary backup, 150 MiB for code, installed packages and bounded logs, and 62 MiB free. This is tight and unproven. Multiple retained backups must live in separate approved free EU storage. Daily consistent backups need an assigned operator or school scheduler because the free host lacks scheduled tasks. Test restoration and delete the temporary copy after verified transfer. Retention must also age out backups.

Pilot estimate: one 30-student class, two sessions per day and 30 teaching days gives 1,800 attendance rows, 1,800 snapshot rows and roughly 180 correction rows. Budget 10 MiB for its database, then measure actual disk use. These are sizing assumptions, not approved retention periods.

Forty teacher views polling every five seconds would make eight requests per second. The chosen four-second interval makes ten. With 1,200 check-ins over one minute, add 20 check-in requests per second, before login and page loads. Assuming a 10 KiB list response, polling alone transfers about 59 MiB over ten minutes at full size. The one-view pilot needs 0.25 polling requests per second and about 1.5 MiB over ten minutes; 30 check-ins over a minute add 0.5 requests per second on average. A classroom burst can be much sharper.

Before real use, test the proposed one-class, 30-student, one-view limit on the actual host and school Wi-Fi, including simultaneous submissions and login. Require no lost or duplicate attendance, correct deadline rejection, list updates within five seconds and a successful restore. Reduce the limit or keep the demo invented if it fails. Department-wide use requires a separate full-load test.

Use invented records on developer laptops. Agree retention and approved EU export devices before importing students. Keep exports out of personal cloud folders.

parts.summary: Prefer school login, check permissions on the server and keep student data in approved EU locations. Use invented students until these conditions are met.
parts.details:
Adam handles browser security work with JavaScript. Sara handles server rules with Python and SQL. Yassine handles Wi-Fi checks, guidance and supervised operational checks using his HTML/CSS background. Security work uses 28 hours already inside T1 and T4–T9: Sara 16, Adam 8 and Yassine 4. It is not an extra allocation. Their complete planned totals remain 33, 33 and 34 hours, with 15, 15 and 14 hours reserved respectively.

Complete basic login, roster membership and teacher-assignment checks in week 2. Students check in only for themselves and enrolled classes. Assigned teachers open sessions, view lists, correct attendance and export CSV. Check every request on the server. Use the server clock for the ten-minute deadline and allow one attendance record per student per session. Record correction reasons, editor and time. Test broader denied-access cases in weeks 4–6.

T4 explicitly covers repeated failed-login limits per account. With school login, Sara verifies the school provider’s protection and configures the app’s applicable login endpoints; Adam tests the integration and failure messages. Do not count normal class check-ins as login failures. Avoid a low shared-IP limit: many students use the same school network address. T9 includes valid classroom logins alongside repeated failures against a separate invented account, checking that unrelated students can still log in. If the provider cannot demonstrate suitable protection, real-account use waits.

Use HTTPS, which encrypts browser traffic, protected session cookies and request protection against forms sent from other sites. Keep secrets outside source code. Validate inputs, protect CSV values that could be read as spreadsheet formulas, and review dependencies. Keep names and session codes out of logs and disable external analytics.

Use an expiring classroom code, while explaining that sharing it remains possible. Teachers still need spot checks and manual corrections. Identify this app clearly even though its pages resemble the school’s site.

Agree minimal data, deletion dates and approved EU export devices. Restrict and encrypt backups, keeping keys separate. Test restoration. On a suspected leak, restrict access, revoke affected sessions and promptly contact the school’s data-protection contact.

parts.summary: Use simple school-style pages for student phones and teacher laptops. Make check-in confirmation, connection problems and corrections clear.
parts.details:
Build four main screens: teacher class list, live session, student check-in and confirmation. The live session shows the roster, attendance counts, closing time, manual corrections and CSV export.

Teacher path: choose class → open session → watch attendance. Student path: open the short address → sign in → enter code → confirm class → check in → see receipt. If the optional QR code is ready, scanning it replaces typing the address and code. A QR code is a camera-readable link. Both routes still require login and enrolment checks.

Use 16px body text, strong contrast, visible keyboard focus and labelled controls. Never rely on colour alone. Show success only after the server confirms saving. Show the deadline and explain how to ask the teacher for a correction if a phone or Wi-Fi fails.

Reuse shared Django page templates, which are HTML layouts filled by the server, and plain JavaScript controls. Yassine owns shared HTML/CSS. Adam owns browser interactions. Sara supplies the server data fields. Use local assets to fit the free budget and avoid outside asset requests.

T10–T14 contain all 24 design hours: Yassine 21 and Adam 3. These are included in the 100-hour delivery budget. Within T13’s six hours, Yassine spends one hour on a simple name-free join display and three on teacher layouts; Adam spends one hour wiring the display and one hour on optional local QR generation. The join display contains only the address, code and closing time. It does not load or show roster names.

The typed-code flow and name-free display are required. At the end of week 3, keep QR only if it is implemented and checked within its one-hour allowance and required flows are on schedule. Otherwise postpone it. Do not add a separate QR service or spend reserve hours on it.

options.bad: More typing and possible mistakes.
options.fit: Automatic fallback if QR exceeds its allowance or required work slips.

problems.problem: The 12 learning hours and 70 hours of architecture tasks are not mapped to the 100-hour delivery plan. Saying learning leaves 132 hours treats the reserved buffer as available work time.
problems.fix: Map these tasks into the delivery plan, name an owner for each, and include learning within roughly 100 planned hours. Keep each person within 48 hours including their buffer.

problems.problem: The 28 security hours have no named owners, and it is unclear which replace existing tasks. Sara already has 33 planned hours, so assigning all this work to her would exceed her 48 hours.
problems.fix: Assign each task to Adam, Sara or Yassine, identify overlapping delivery tasks, and count each task once in the shared hour totals.

problems.problem: The plan has no observable completion checks for the required features. The team cannot tell consistently when a feature is finished.
problems.fix: Add checks for opening a session, accepting an enrolled student's check-in before the deadline and rejecting it afterward, updating the teacher list within five seconds, saving a manual correction, and downloading the correct class CSV.

problems.problem: “Use framework login” does not settle whether students use school login or local passwords. Local accounts would add password storage, provisioning and recovery work that is not covered here.
problems.fix: Make school login the conditional first choice. If it is unavailable, keep the demo on invented accounts until local-account setup, slow password hashing and school-verified recovery have named owners and budgeted hours.

problems.problem: Login failure limits are described as an action, but no task explicitly implements them. Framework login alone does not establish those limits.
problems.fix: Include account-based failed-login limits in the authentication task, with a classroom burst test that checks shared school Wi-Fi does not block legitimate users.

problems.problem: The hosting section names free-plan limits but never estimates storage or traffic against them. A proposed load test alone does not establish whether the pilot fits.
problems.fix: Estimate attendance rows and disk use from explicit session and retention assumptions. Include backups in the 512 MiB allowance and the eight polling requests per second from 40 teacher views. Set a tested pilot size before real use.

problems.problem: The reference to React shared controls conflicts with the chosen Django pages and small JavaScript functions. Adding React would introduce unbudgeted setup and learning.
problems.fix: Specify shared Django page templates and plain JavaScript controls. Keep Yassine responsible for shared HTML/CSS and Adam for browser interactions.

problems.problem: Access checks are scheduled to finish in week 4, but students and teachers need working login and permissions for the week-3 attendance flow.
problems.fix: Move basic login, roster membership and teacher-assignment checks into week 2. Keep broader denied-access testing in weeks 4–6.

problems.problem: QR generation and a separate join-only view add work without showing where it fits in Adam's and Yassine's existing hours.
problems.fix: Include both in named, budgeted tasks and define a cutoff: if they do not fit, use a typed code with a simple name-free join display and postpone QR generation.

sections.details: Where real student data may run: school EU hosting offers support but needs confirmation; verified free EU hosting costs nothing but needs destination/capacity checks; invented-data demonstration meets day 42 but cannot serve classes. Test department demand before expanding. Keep existing attendance procedures available.

pushBacks.idea: Launch the whole department on free hosting by week 6.
pushBacks.problem: Capacity, access and EU handling of login, logs and backups are unconfirmed.
pushBacks.better: Approve hosting and test a small pilot; use invented data if prerequisites fail.

pushBacks.problem: Codes and accounts can be shared; Wi-Fi proves no presence.
pushBacks.better: Require login, membership, teacher spot checks and recorded corrections.

pushBacks.idea: Every present student must check in by phone within ten minutes.
pushBacks.problem: Dead phones or failed Wi-Fi prevent submission.
pushBacks.better: Keep the deadline; offer teacher-assisted corrections.

choices.question: Who approves EU hosting, login, rosters, retention, exports and backup ownership? Can access arrive in week 1?
options: School arrangements: supported real use; availability unconfirmed.
Verified free arrangements: no spending; approval and operations consume hours.
Invented-data demo: meets deadline; provides no attendance service.

choices.question: Which teacher, class and Wi-Fi slot are available? What simultaneous department demand needs later support?
options: One teacher, up to 30 students: manageable; limited capacity evidence.
Smaller class: easier coordination; weaker traffic evidence.
Invented classroom test: avoids approvals; misses classroom behaviour.

choices.question: Which visual reference should Yassine follow?
options: School style guide: consistent; requires access.
Existing school page: quick; may lack accessibility guidance.

choices.question: Does the teacher accept check-ins with spot checks and corrections?
options: Yes: fits scope; shared-code cheating remains possible.
No: retain existing attendance; demonstration helps, but requirements need revision.

decision.title: How broadly to launch by week 6

options.name: Small classroom pilot
options.good: Tests the complete flow on school Wi-Fi with manageable support.
options.bad: Does not prove department-wide capacity.
options.fit: Fits the 100 planned hours, subject to school approval and passing tests.

options.name: Immediate department-wide launch
options.good: All teachers and students can benefit immediately.
options.bad: Adds uncertain traffic, account setup, training and support.
options.fit: Too risky to promise within six weeks and a free-only budget.

decision.why: Build for the department, but expand only after testing access, Wi-Fi and simultaneous check-ins.

decision.title: Where real student data may run

options.name: School-provided EU hosting
options.good: May include approved backups and a support contact.
options.bad: Free capacity, HTTPS and access remain unconfirmed.
options.fit: Preferred if school IT can provide it promptly.

options.name: Verified free EU service
options.good: Could meet the budget.
options.bad: Needs checks on processing, logs, backups, support access and limits.
options.fit: Use real data only after school approval covers every destination.

options.name: Invented-data demo
options.good: Preserves the week-6 demonstration without exposing student records.
options.bad: Does not provide a live department rollout.
options.fit: Required fallback if hosting or identity remains unresolved.

decision.why: An EU database setting alone does not establish that the whole service meets the EU-only rule.

decision.title: Account identity

options.name: School login
options.good: School handles identity, passwords and recovery.
options.bad: Needs access and a compatible integration.
options.fit: Conditional first choice within T1 and T4.

options.name: Local accounts
options.good: Can operate without school login integration.
options.bad: Adds provisioning, password storage, recovery and support.
options.fit: Invented demo accounts only until real-account work has owners and an approved hour budget.

decision.why: The 100-hour plan does not fund a real local-account service.

decision.title: Free hosting with EU storage

options.name: School-managed EU server
options.good: May provide storage, backups and support without spending.
options.bad: Availability and capacity are unknown.
options.fit: First choice if school IT confirms it in week 1.

options.name: PythonAnywhere EU free service
options.good: Offers a Python app and persistent storage for a demo.
options.bad: Limited worker and disk capacity, expiry and no scheduled tasks for new free accounts.
options.fit: Conditional demo or tested small pilot only; school approval must cover all data destinations.

decision.why: School support is preferable, but not assumed. Use invented data if no approved free arrangement exists.

decision.title: Application structure

options.name: Django pages with SQLite
options.good: One project with built-in forms, sessions and database tools.
options.bad: Django needs learning; SQLite permits one writer at a time.
options.fit: Uses Sara’s Python, Adam’s JavaScript and Yassine’s HTML/CSS with 12 planned learning hours.

options.name: React front end and Python API
options.good: Uses Adam’s React experience.
options.bad: Adds separate builds and more login integration.
options.fit: Too much setup for the six-week schedule.

decision.why: Simple forms and a changing list fit one application. Test short simultaneous writes before expanding.

decision.title: How students reach the session

options.name: Typed code, with optional QR shortcut
options.good: Always offers camera-free entry; QR can reduce typing.
options.bad: QR adds generation and scan checks.
options.fit: Typed entry is committed. QR gets at most one Adam hour within T13 and a week-3 cutoff.

options.name: Typed code only
options.good: Few controls and no camera dependency.
options.bad: More typing and possible mistakes.
options.fit: Automatic fallback if QR exceeds its allowance or required work slips.

decision.picked: Typed code, with optional QR shortcut
decision.why: Both routes use the same protected check-in page. Show the class before submission and keep identity checks separate from the code.

decision.title: How people log in

options.name: School login
options.good: The school handles passwords, identity and recovery.
options.bad: Needs school approval, integration access and verified failure protection.
options.fit: First choice for 1,240 people within the six-week, free-only plan.

options.name: School-provisioned local accounts
options.good: Can work without school login integration.
options.bad: Adds account setup, slow password hashing, school-verified recovery and support.
options.fit: Real accounts require a revised budget with named owners; until then use invented demo accounts.

decision.why: Confirm integration and EU handling in week 1. Do not quietly add a real local-password service to the existing schedule.
